title: ATM races and failure cases
idea: ATM concurrency means two withdrawals on one account must never both pass the balance check, and every failure after a debit must end in exactly one reversal.

analogy.text: Two flatmates share one cash jar. Each checks it in the morning, sees enough, and promises a shop to pay later.
analogy.breaks: A real jar cannot go negative; an unguarded balance field can.

points: Check-then-debit is two steps; another ATM can debit between them.
`compareAndSet` writes only if the balance is still what this thread read.
A request id makes a retried debit return the first result, not debit again.
A jam after the debit triggers `reverse`; only a PENDING transaction can reverse.

steps.caption: Unsafe version. Both cardholders ask for Rs 800 from Rs 1,000 at the same moment.
Both threads read the balance before either writes. Both see enough.
ATM-1 debits. The balance drops to Rs 200.
ATM-2 acts on its stale yes and debits too. The account is now negative.
Safe version. Each thread calls `compareAndSet`, expecting the balance it read.
One swap succeeds and writes Rs 200. The other finds the value changed and fails.
The loser reads again, sees Rs 200 is not enough, and refuses. The account never goes negative.

code.title: The race and the fix
code.caption: A barrier forces both threads to check before either acts, so the bad outcome repeats on every run.

walk.text: One balance, a barrier for two threads, and a counter of approvals.
Unsafe: check, wait for the other ATM, then debit on a stale answer.
Safe: both start together, but each debit is one atomic step.
Read, check, and swap only if unchanged; on a lost swap, loop and re-check.
Join both threads before printing, so the output is always the same.

code.title: Lost reply and jam
code.caption: Two failure cases: the bank's reply is lost and the ATM retries; then the notes jam and the debit is reversed.

walk.text: The first debit succeeds and is PENDING until the cash leaves.
The ATM never got the reply. It retries with the same request id.
A known request id returns the first transaction. No second debit.
The notes jam. The ATM sends `reverse` twice, as a retry would.
Only a PENDING transaction can reverse, so the money returns once.
A late `confirm` after the reversal is refused, not applied.

pitfalls: A Java lock guards one process; across many bank servers, lock the database row.
Never retry a debit without the same request id; a timeout may hide a success.
If some notes left before a jam, reverse only the part that stayed inside.

quiz.q: What does BalanceRace print for check-then-debit?
quiz.why: Both threads check before the barrier, while the balance is 100000. After it, both subtract 80000, leaving minus 60000.

takeaway: Make the check and the debit one step; make retries and reversals idempotent.

starters: When is synchronized better than compareAndSet here?
How long should the ATM wait before it calls reverse?
What if the ATM loses power between debit and dispense?
